Hurricane · next 24 hours

Rapid intensification: the chance in the next 24 hours

Rapid intensification means a tropical cyclone’s maximum sustained winds rise by 30 knots or more within 24 hours — the kind of change official forecasts find hardest to anticipate. For each active storm we publish the best available probability: NOAA’s own guidance where it exists, our model elsewhere. Each storm names its source.

Where each number comes from

Atlantic, East and Central Pacific. NOAA’s own probability, read from the National Hurricane Center’s SHIPS text for the same forecast cycle: DTOPS as issued, or SHIPS-RII when DTOPS is missing. We chose it in a comparison written down in advance and run on 2020–2024, then scored it once on the 2025 season: it ranked a cycle that went on to intensify rapidly above one that did not 92.8% of the time over 601 forecast cycles and 33 storms, and beat NOAA SHIPS-RII, NOAA RIOC consensus and our previous model (v8.2) on the same cycles.

West Pacific, Indian Ocean and Southern Hemisphere, where no public rapid-intensification guidance exists, and any NHC cycle without usable SHIPS text: our v8.2 model. Its method was tested on 8,317 forecast cycles from 2022–2024 in every basin (South Indian 2,245, West Pacific 2,110, Atlantic 1,521, East Pacific 1,288, South Pacific 673, North Indian 480), none of them used to fit it: it ranked a cycle that went on to intensify rapidly above one that did not 84.7% of the time. That test read each storm’s inputs from the best track, and the model now published is the same method refitted with its calibration fitted on those same cycles, so the figure is not a test of the published model on unseen data. In the West Pacific, Indian Ocean and southern hemisphere a storm’s recent track comes from the working best track (UCAR RAL’s real-time copy), the kind of track the model was trained on before its post-season revision. Scored from a single JTWC warning instead — which leaves 9 of its 17 inputs unknown, as it did until 2026-10-05 and still does if that file cannot be read — the 2022–2024 West Pacific cycles had a log loss of 0.259, against 0.265 for always forecasting the average (0.206 with every input). When a cycle’s best-track fix is not yet published, the warning is the analysis and the storm’s central pressure and its changes are filled with typical values: scored that way, 0.213.

Read the full test

Our experimental model

HazardPulse v10.1 is our own rapid-intensification model, built from NOAA’s intensity guidance, its rapid-intensification probabilities and the official forecast. Over the 2022–2025 seasons, each forecast only from earlier seasons, it scored better than DTOPS: log loss 0.144 against 0.165 (lower is better).

That is not yet proof. It is shown beside NOAA’s number, never instead of it, while a test written down in advance scores it on new forecasts; the verdicts are due on 1 Dec 2026 and 1 Dec 2027. Forecast cycles scored so far: 8.
